title: Tenant-adaptive deferred-admission buffer and decay fallback for limiter outages
creator: Maya Chen
description: Customers observed hard failures when regional limiter control planes experienced transient outages during multi-region failover. Current shedding is aggressive and can spike tail latency or drop important requests. Proposal: implement a tenant-adaptive deferred-admission buffer with exponential decay and emergency eviction that integrates with circuit-breaker state. Goal is to preserve SLOs for high-priority tenants while allowing graceful degradation and rapid recovery during limiter outages.
acceptance_criteria: When control-plane loss occurs in a region, incoming requests are admitted into an in-memory deferred buffer per-tenant up to configured soft and hard caps
Buffer admission respects tenant priority weights and SLO-derived protection thresholds (e.g., reserve 20% capacity for P0/P1 tenants)
Deferred requests are either admitted into runtime when capacity is available or evicted according to configured decay and fairness policy within 30s by default
System exposes realtime buffer metrics and allows operator-driven emergency-evict via Console and CLI
No regression in p95 latency for normal (non-failing) traffic patterns after rollout
implementation_notes: Add per-tenant circular buffers co-located with proxy edge nodes; buffer entries store request metadata and short-lived token pointers, not payloads
Admission policy: prefer immediate processing; if runtime admission fails, attempt deferred buffering if tenant has unused soft quota and buffer not full
Decay policy: time-decay factor plus token-cost decay (older entries and larger token requests are evicted first)
Integrate with existing circuit-breaker: when circuit trips for a downstream pool, buffer enters emergency mode with stricter hard caps and prioritized eviction
Implement a lightweight backpressure header to inform SDKs/clients when request was deferred (x-rw-deferred: true) to help client-side UX and retries
Ensure buffer memory accounting and graceful GC — max 1.5GB per proxy in default config, with tenant-level overrides for enterprise customers
decisions: Use in-memory per-proxy buffers rather than centralized queue to avoid cross-region latency and single points of failure
Prioritize tenants by SLO-derived weight (combine committed throughput and recent error budget burn) rather than static tier alone
Expose operator controls in Console for manual emergency-evict and buffer-size tuning; default to automatic decay
Do not persist request bodies in buffer; instead store pointers and short-lived KV cache refs to enforce data residency policies
tradeoffs: Pros: reduces 500 errors during transient control-plane limiter outages, preserves high-priority tenant SLOs, faster failback
Cons: increased memory footprint on edge proxies, more complex admission logic, potential for small increases in tail latency for deferred requests
Security: keeping pointers instead of payloads avoids persistent PII storage but adds dependency on short-lived KV caches; this complicates private/vpc deployments where cache placement differs
testing_plan: Unit tests for admission and eviction heuristics with synthetic tenant weight distributions
Chaos test: kill control-plane limiter for a region in staging while driving mixed-priority traffic; validate no >3% increase in 5xx for P0 tenants
Load test: scale to 10k rps with 30% bursty tenants to validate memory caps and eviction behavior
Integration test: verify circuit-breaker state transitions trigger buffer emergency mode and that Console emergency-evict succeeds
E2E test with SDK: verify client receives x-rw-deferred header and that retry guidance avoids thundering-herd
rollout_plan: Feature gated behind runtime-flag; enable for 10% of proxies in staging for 48h
Canary: 5% of proxies in prod region-a with synthetic traffic watchdog and dashboards; monitor for 72h
Gradual ramp: 25% then 50% then 100% over rolling 2-week window if no regressions
Release includes Console toggle and alerting thresholds; Ops playbook to manually evict buffers during unforeseen behavior
In case of severe regressions, feature can be disabled via runtime flag to revert behavior within 1 minute
